Edochie, aged 79, died at 12:30am on Wednesday, November 25, 2026, in Enugu State, after a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.
His death was announced in a statement signed by his son, Chief Leo Pete Edochie, on behalf of the family.
The family described the deceased as a beloved husband, father, brother and kinsman, adding that funeral arrangements would be communicated in due course.
Edochie’s death has once again highlighted the importance of understanding prostate cancer, recognising its warning signs and seeking medical attention early.
Prostate cancer is a type of cancer that develops in the prostate gland, a small gland found in men below the bladder and in front of the rectum.
The gland produces fluid that forms part of semen and plays an important role in male reproductive health.
The disease occurs when cells in the prostate begin to grow uncontrollably, potentially forming a tumour that can spread to other parts of the body if not detected and treated.
Although some prostate cancers grow slowly, others can develop aggressively and spread beyond the prostate.
Although all men can develop prostate cancer, certain factors increase the likelihood of developing the disease.
Age is one of the biggest risk factors, with the chances increasing as men grow older.
One of the challenges associated with prostate cancer is that it may not produce noticeable symptoms during its early stages.
These symptoms do not necessarily mean someone has prostate cancer, as other prostate and urinary conditions can produce similar signs.
However, men experiencing persistent symptoms should seek medical evaluation.
Yes. Prostate cancer can spread beyond the prostate gland to other parts of the body.
The cancer can spread to nearby tissues, lymph nodes and distant organs, particularly the bones.
When the disease advances, affected individuals may experience persistent pain in the back, hips or pelvis.
Other possible symptoms include unexplained weight loss, fatigue and weakness.
The extent to which the cancer has spread is an important factor doctors consider when determining treatment options.
Doctors use different medical procedures to establish whether a patient has prostate cancer.
One of the major methods is the Prostate-Specific Antigen (PSA) blood test.
The test measures the level of a protein produced by the prostate gland. Elevated PSA levels may indicate prostate cancer, although other conditions, including prostate enlargement and inflammation, can also cause an increase.
An elevated PSA result alone does not confirm prostate cancer. Further medical evaluation is necessary.
Yes. The Prostate-Specific Antigen blood test is the main screening method used to identify possible prostate cancer before symptoms develop.
However, screening decisions should be discussed with a qualified healthcare professional because the test has limitations and can sometimes produce abnormal results in men who do not have cancer.
The American Cancer Society recommends that men discuss screening with their doctors, particularly from age 50 for those at average risk and age 45 for those at higher risk, including Black men.
Men with a strong family history may need to discuss screening even earlier.
Yes. Prostate cancer can be treated, and the appropriate treatment depends on the stage of the disease, how aggressive it is, the patient’s age and general health.
Doctors determine the most appropriate treatment after assessing the patient’s condition.
There is currently no guaranteed way to prevent prostate cancer.
However, maintaining a healthy lifestyle may help improve overall health and potentially reduce some risk factors.
These measures do not guarantee protection against prostate cancer.
Early detection is important because prostate cancer identified before it spreads may offer patients more treatment options and better chances of successful management.
Some prostate cancers grow slowly and may not require immediate treatment, while aggressive forms can spread quickly.
Regular medical consultations and appropriate screening discussions can help identify suspicious changes before the disease advances.
Men should also avoid ignoring persistent urinary problems or assuming they are simply a normal consequence of ageing.
Men should seek medical attention if they experience persistent urinary difficulties, blood in their urine or semen, unexplained pelvic pain or other unusual symptoms.
Those with a family history of prostate cancer should also discuss their risk with a healthcare professional.
Medical advice is particularly important for men above 40 who have additional risk factors, including African ancestry and a family history of the disease.
Although prostate cancer is a serious health condition, an early medical assessment can make a significant difference in diagnosis and treatment.
Edochie’s death serves as another reminder of the importance of men’s health awareness and timely medical attention.
